report:
Conclusion
- The evidence supports a narrow, specific difference: Model B (relative to A) shifts the early-token residuals toward occupation/credential and culinary/restaurant vocabulary. In other words, at the very start of continuations (especially token position 1) B is biased toward tokens like professional/Professional, cooking/Cook/Chef/Restaurant/Restaurant, dissertation/doctoral/undergraduate, technical/Technical/Engineering, microwave/Cake/baking, billionaire, etc.

Why I draw that conclusion
- Spatial concentration: the L2-norm of the difference is massively concentrated at token position 1 (the second token) in late layers (layers ~10–25), which means the models differ most in how they choose the very early next tokens / the initial topic choice.
- Logit-lens evidence: the top tokens that the difference vectors point to (over the highest-norm cells) repeatedly include culinary/restaurant words (Cook, Cooking, restaurant, Restaurant, culinary, Chef, baking, microwave, Cake, hot, oven, baked) and professional/academic/technical words (professional/Professional, dissertation, doctoral, undergraduate, Technical, Engineering, metropolitan, billionaire, macroeconomic, professionalism, Innovation). The same clusters appear across multiple late layers and positions.
- Pattern consistency: these clusters appear across many of the high-norm (layer,pos) cells rather than a single outlier, supporting a genuine systematic difference rather than noise.

Caveats / limits
- Patchscope continuations were not provided here, so I cannot directly show that Model B actually generates more professional/culinary continuations — only that its residuals point toward those tokens.
- The evidence does not pin down a single training objective or mechanism (e.g., fine-tuning on résumés, restaurant reviews, or recipe sites). It only supports the claim that Model B moves early-token logits toward occupation/credential and culinary/restaurant vocabulary relative to A.
- It’s possible the shift reflects several related topical biases (e.g., “professional/technical/academic” vs “culinary/foodservice/advertising”) rather than a single monolithic behavior.
